questions.question: Number of particles in the unit cell of a simple cube is
questions.answer:
**(A)** 1

In a simple cubic (primitive) unit cell the atoms sit only at the eight corners, and each corner atom is shared by eight adjoining cells:

$$n=8\times\frac18=1$$

So there is exactly one particle per unit cell; the packing fraction is only 52%, the lowest of the cubic lattices (b.c.c. has 2, f.c.c. has 4).

questions.question: Which of the following aqueous solutions has the highest boiling point?
questions.answer:
**(D)** 1% CaCl$_2$

Boiling point depends on the number of particles (van't Hoff factor). For equal mass percentages, the solute of lowest molar mass gives the most moles; but the decisive factor here is ionisation: glucose and sucrose do not ionise ($i=1$), NaCl gives 2 ions, CaCl$_2$ gives 3. Since CaCl$_2$ (M = 111) also has a low molar mass, 1% CaCl$_2$ gives both the most moles and the largest $i$, hence the greatest elevation $\Delta T_b=iK_bm$ and the highest boiling point.

questions.question: Emulsion is a colloidal solution of
questions.answer:
**(B)** two liquids

An emulsion is a colloidal dispersion of one liquid in another immiscible liquid — milk (fat droplets in water) and mayonnaise (water in oil) are the familiar examples. A small amount of an emulsifying agent (soap, proteins) stabilises the droplets. Dispersions of a solid in a liquid are called sols, not emulsions.

questions.question: Which of the following Noble gases is most reactive?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Xe

Down the noble-gas group the ionisation energy falls and the outer electrons become less tightly held, so chemical reactivity increases in the order He < Ne < Ar < Kr < Xe < Rn. Xenon (and to a lesser extent krypton) forms real compounds with the most electronegative elements — XeF$_2$, XeF$_4$, XeF$_6$, XeO$_3$ — while helium and neon form none.

questions.question: Which of the following forms coloured salt?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Fe$^{2+}$

Colour in transition-metal ions arises from $d$–$d$ transitions, which need a partly filled $d$ subshell. Fe$^{2+}$ is $3d^6$ and is coloured (pale green). Cu$^+$ is $3d^{10}$, Zn$^{2+}$ is $3d^{10}$ and Ag$^+$ is $4d^{10}$ — all completely filled, all colourless. The printed key marks (a) Cu$^+$, but that ion is colourless and Fe$^{2+}$ is the only coloured one listed.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds is optically active?
questions.answer:
**(B)** 2-butanol

Optical activity requires a chiral centre — a carbon bearing four different groups. In 2-butanol, C-2 carries $\ce{-H}$, $\ce{-OH}$, $\ce{-CH3}$ and $\ce{-C2H5}$: four different groups, so the molecule is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers. 1-Butanol and 1-propanol are achiral (the carbinol carbon carries two H), and 2-propanol also has two identical methyl groups.

questions.question: Lucas test is used to distinguish
questions.answer:
**(A)** Alcohols

The Lucas test uses Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl$_2$) and distinguishes $1^\circ$, $2^\circ$ and $3^\circ$ alcohols by the time taken for the mixture to turn turbid, which marks the formation of the insoluble alkyl chloride: tertiary alcohols react at once, secondary within about 5 minutes, primary only on heating. (The printed key marks (c) amines, which is incorrect — amines are distinguished by the Hinsberg test.)

questions.question: Which of the following amines forms alcohol on treatment with HNO$_2$?
questions.answer:
**(A)** CH$_3$-NH$_2$

A primary aliphatic amine reacts with nitrous acid to give an unstable diazonium salt which decomposes immediately, liberating nitrogen and leaving the **alcohol**:

$$\ce{CH3NH2 + HNO2 -> CH3OH + N2 + H2O}$$

Secondary amines give yellow oily N-nitrosamines, and tertiary amines give nitrite salts that dissolve. (Aniline, though primary, gives a stable diazonium salt in the cold and yields phenol only on warming.)

*Note on the printed key:* the paper marks (c), the tertiary amine, which does not give an alcohol.

questions.question: Can we separate the components of an azeotropic mixture by fractional distillation?
questions.answer:
**(B)** No

An azeotrope boils at a constant temperature and distils with a constant composition — its vapour has the same composition as the liquid. Fractional distillation works only if the vapour is richer in the more volatile component, so it cannot separate an azeotrope; special methods such as pressure-swing distillation or extractive/azeotropic distillation with a third component are needed. Ethanol–water at 95.6% is the classic example.

questions.question: Complete the following: $\ce{C6H5-Br + CH3-Br + Na ->[dry ether]}$
questions.answer:
This is the **Wurtz–Fittig reaction** — an aryl halide and an alkyl halide couple in the presence of sodium in dry ether:

$$\ce{C6H5Br + CH3Br + 2Na ->[dry ether] C6H5CH3 + NaBr}$$

The product is **toluene** (methylbenzene). Sodium supplies electrons that generate aryl and alkyl radicals (or organosodium species), which combine; using only an aryl halide would need the Wurtz reaction, and mixtures of products form if two different alkyl halides are used, so one component is usually taken as the aryl halide.

questions.question: Complete the following: $\ce{C6H5OH + Br2 ->[H2O]}$
questions.answer:
Bromine water reacts at once with phenol — no catalyst and no heating are needed, because the —OH group strongly activates the ring towards electrophilic substitution. A **white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol** is formed:

$$\ce{C6H5OH + 3Br2(aq) -> 2,4,6-Br3C6H2OH v + 3HBr}$$

The immediate decolourisation of bromine water with a white precipitate is the standard test for phenol. With a low concentration of bromine or in a non-polar solvent, mono- and di-bromophenols can be isolated.

questions.question: Write down the I.U.P.A.C. name of $\ce{CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CO-CH3}$.
questions.answer:
**4-Methylpentan-2-one.**

The longest chain containing the ketone carbonyl has five carbons, numbered so that the carbonyl carbon is C-2; the methyl branch then falls on C-4:

$$\ce{CH3-CO-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH3}$$

so the name is 4-methylpentan-2-one (trivial name: methyl isobutyl ketone).

questions.question: Write down the number of 1$^\circ$ amines having molecular formula C$_4$H$_{11}$N (only structural isomers).
questions.answer:
**4 structural isomers.**

All are primary amines, $\ce{R-NH2}$, with the four-carbon skeletons available:

1. butan-1-amine, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2}$
2. butan-2-amine, $\ce{CH3CH2CH(NH2)CH3}$
3. 2-methylpropan-1-amine, $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2NH2}$
4. 2-methylpropan-2-amine (tert-butylamine), $\ce{(CH3)3CNH2}$

(Counting all amines of this formula would give 8, since secondary and tertiary isomers also exist: N-methylpropan-1-amine, N-methylpropan-2-amine, N-ethylethanamine and N,N-dimethylethanamine.)

questions.question: Write down the name of a monosaccharide.
questions.answer:
**Glucose** — $\ce{C6H12O6}$, an aldohexose, the most abundant monosaccharide and the body's main energy source.

*(Galactose and fructose, $\ce{C6H12O6}$, and ribose, $\ce{C5H10O5}$, are other monosaccharides; fructose is a ketohexose.)* Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed to simpler sugars and are the monomer units of all di- and polysaccharides.

questions.question: Write down the name of an antipyretic drug.
questions.answer:
**Paracetamol** (acetaminophen) — the most widely used antipyretic and mild analgesic; it lowers fever by acting on the hypothalamic temperature-regulating centre.

*(Other common antipyretics: **aspirin** (acetylsalicylic acid) and **phenacetin**.)* Antipyretics differ from antibiotics in that they do not kill micro-organisms — they relieve the symptom of fever.

questions.question: State and explain Kohlrausch's law.
questions.answer:
**Kohlrausch's law (law of independent migration of ions):** at infinite dilution, when dissociation is complete and interionic effects vanish, the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its individual ions:

$$\Lambda_m^\infty=\nu_+\lambda_+^\infty+\nu_-\lambda_-^\infty$$

where $\nu_+$ and $\nu_-$ are the numbers of cations and anions produced by one formula unit, and $\lambda_+^\infty$, $\lambda_-^\infty$ are the limiting ionic conductivities.

**Explanation:** on infinite dilution the ions are so far apart that each migrates independently of the other and contributes a fixed amount to the total conductance, irrespective of the partner ion. This is why $\Lambda_m^\infty$ values of strong electrolytes can be combined additively. The law is particularly useful for **weak electrolytes**, whose $\Lambda_m^\infty$ cannot be found by extrapolation:

$$\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{CH3COOH})=\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{CH3COONa})+\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{HCl})-\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{NaCl})$$

It also gives the degree of dissociation, $\alpha=\Lambda_m/\Lambda_m^\infty$, and hence the dissociation constant of a weak acid.

questions.question: Give balanced equation of the following: (i) $\ce{H2S + H2SO4(conc)}$ (ii) $\ce{NaHCO3 + H2SO4(dilute)}$
questions.answer:
**(i) Hydrogen sulphide with concentrated sulphuric acid** — sulphuric acid is reduced to sulphur dioxide while sulphide is oxidised to sulphur:

$$\ce{H2S + H2SO4(conc) -> 2SO2 + 2H2O + S}$$

(Equivalently $\ce{H2S + H2SO4 -> S v + SO2 ^ + 2H2O}$.) Concentrated sulphuric acid therefore acts as an oxidising agent towards $\ce{H2S}$.

**(ii) Sodium bicarbonate with dilute sulphuric acid** — a simple acid–carbonate reaction giving the sulphate, carbon dioxide and water:

$$\ce{2NaHCO3 + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2CO2 ^ + 2H2O}$$

The brisk effervescence of CO$_2$ is the visible sign of the reaction.

questions.question: Give balance equation of the following: (i) $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-} + I^- + H^+}$ (ii) $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-} + Fe^{2+} + H^+}$
questions.answer:
In acid medium dichromate is reduced to Cr(III) (green), each chromium falling from +6 to +3 — a gain of 3 electrons per Cr, 6 per $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$.

**(i) With iodide**, which is oxidised to iodine (each I$^-$ loses one electron):

$$\ce{Cr2O7^{2-} + 6I^- + 14H^+ -> 2Cr^{3+} + 3I2 + 7H2O}$$

**(ii) With iron(II)**, oxidised to iron(III):

$$\ce{Cr2O7^{2-} + 6Fe^{2+} + 14H^+ -> 2Cr^{3+} + 6Fe^{3+} + 7H2O}$$

Both are used quantitatively — the first in iodometric titration, the second in the dichromate titration of ferrous iron (with diphenylamine as indicator).

questions.question: What is Lanthanide contraction? What are its effects?
questions.answer:
**Lanthanoid contraction** is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series (La to Lu) with increasing atomic number.

**Cause:** as $Z$ increases by one, the extra electron enters the deep 4f subshell, which shields the outer electrons from the nucleus very poorly. The effective nuclear charge therefore rises steadily and draws the outer shells in.

**Effects**

1. **Similarity of the members** — because the radii change only slightly, all lanthanoids have very similar chemical properties and are difficult to separate (ion-exchange and solvent extraction are needed).
2. **Zr and Hf are almost identical in size** (the contraction cancels the expected increase from the third to the fourth period), so they occur together and are hard to separate.
3. **The 4d and 5d transition series resemble each other** closely for the same reason.
4. It causes the **basicity of the lanthanoid hydroxides to decrease** from La(OH)$_3$ to Lu(OH)$_3$, and explains some anomalies in ionisation enthalpies.

questions.question: Distinguish between the following with the help of one chemical reaction: (i) Chlorobenzene and benzyl chloride (ii) Chlorobenzene and cyclohexyl chloride
questions.answer:
(i) **Chlorobenzene vs benzyl chloride — hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH.** Benzyl chloride reacts readily (S$_N$1, the benzylic cation is stabilised by the ring) to give benzyl alcohol, while chlorobenzene is inert, because the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character from resonance with the ring:

$$\ce{C6H5CH2Cl + NaOH(aq) ->[\Delta] C6H5CH2OH + NaCl}\quad\text{(reacts)}$$

$$\ce{C6H5Cl + NaOH -> \text{no reaction under mild conditions}}$$

An even quicker test: adding aqueous AgNO$_3$ gives a white precipitate of AgCl at once with benzyl chloride but none with chlorobenzene.

(ii) **Chlorobenzene vs cyclohexyl chloride** — the same hydrolysis test works, but the opposite way is more striking: **cyclohexyl chloride gives a precipitate with AgNO$_3$** (or hydrolyses with aqueous alkali) because its C–Cl bond is a normal $sp^3$ bond, whereas chlorobenzene does not. Chlorobenzene needs the drastic Dow conditions (NaOH, 623 K, high pressure) to be hydrolysed at all.

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) $\ce{R-OH + PCl5}$ (ii) $\ce{R-OH + PCl3}$
questions.answer:
(i) With **phosphorus pentachloride** the hydroxyl group is replaced by chlorine, giving the alkyl chloride, phosphoryl chloride and hydrogen chloride:

$$\ce{R-OH + PCl5 -> R-Cl + POCl3 + HCl}$$

This is the standard laboratory method for converting an alcohol to an alkyl halide.

(ii) With **phosphorus trichloride** two molecules of alcohol are used per $\ce{PCl3}$ (or three for complete conversion of the phosphorus), giving the alkyl chloride and phosphorous acid:

$$\ce{3R-OH + PCl3 -> 3R-Cl + H3PO3}$$

(The printed key writes it with one equivalent, $\ce{R-OH + PCl3 -> R-Cl + POCl3 + HCl}$, which is the $\ce{PCl5}$ stoichiometry.)

questions.question: Aniline is a weaker base than ethyl amine. Explain.
questions.answer:
**Aniline is much weaker than ethylamine** ($\text{p}K_b$ of aniline ≈ 9.4 against ≈ 3.3 for ethylamine) because of three effects acting on the lone pair of nitrogen:

1. **Resonance delocalisation (the dominant reason).** In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the aromatic ring, giving resonance structures in which nitrogen bears a positive charge and the ring a negative one. The lone pair is therefore less available for donation to a proton, so the free base is stabilised and the conjugate acid less so:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + H^+ \rightleftharpoons C6H5NH3^+}$$

2. **Hybridisation.** The aniline nitrogen is closer to $sp^2$ (to allow the lone pair to lie in a p orbital parallel to the ring), whereas in ethylamine it is $sp^3$; greater s character holds the lone pair more tightly.

3. **Inductive effect.** The $sp^2$-rich ring carbons are electron-withdrawing relative to $sp^3$ carbons, further reducing electron density on nitrogen; in ethylamine the alkyl group is electron-releasing (+I), which increases it.

In water, ethylamine is also solvated better through hydrogen bonding of its free lone pair, again making it the stronger base.

questions.question: What is an antibiotic? Name any two antibiotics.
questions.answer:
**Antibiotics** are substances produced wholly or partly by chemical synthesis which, in low concentrations, inhibit the growth of or destroy micro-organisms by interfering with their metabolic processes (cell-wall synthesis, protein synthesis, or nucleic-acid function).

Examples: **penicillin** (blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis) and **streptomycin** (binds to the ribosome and inhibits protein synthesis); others are tetracycline, chloramphenicol, ampicillin and erythromycin. Because they act on processes absent in human cells, they are selectively toxic.

questions.question: Write down three differences between crystalline and amorphous solids.
questions.answer:
| Crystalline solid | Amorphous solid |
|---|---|
| Definite, regular, long-range order of particles | Irregular, random arrangement — no long-range order |
| Sharp, characteristic melting point | Softens gradually over a range of temperature |
| True solid: anisotropic, with a characteristic X-ray diffraction pattern | Pseudo-solid or super-cooled liquid: isotropic, no sharp diffraction pattern |

Examples: NaCl and quartz are crystalline; glass and rubber are amorphous.

questions.question: Define the following terms: (i) Molarity (ii) Molality (iii) Mole fraction.
questions.answer:
**(i) Molarity ($M$)** — the number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution:

$$M=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution in litre}}$$

Its unit is mol L$^{-1}$. It changes with temperature, since volume does.

**(ii) Molality ($m$)** — the number of moles of solute per kilogram of *solvent*:

$$m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}$$

Its unit is mol kg$^{-1}$. Because it involves masses, it is independent of temperature, which is why it is used in colligative-property calculations.

**(iii) Mole fraction ($x$)** — the ratio of the number of moles of one component to the total number of moles in the solution:

$$x_A=\frac{n_A}{n_A+n_B}$$

It is dimensionless and, for a two-component system, $x_A+x_B=1$.

questions.question: What do you understand by standard e.m.f. of a cell? Derive a relationship between standard e.m.f. of a cell and equilibrium constant. / What is the value of electrode potential of Mg$^{2+}$/Mg electrode when it is dipped in a solution in which concentration of Mg$^{2+}$ is 0.01 M? ($E^\circ_{Mg^{2+}/Mg}=-2.36$ V)
questions.answer:
**Standard e.m.f. ($E^\circ_{cell}$)** is the potential difference of a cell when all the species taking part are at unit activity (1 M concentration, 1 bar for gases) and the temperature is 298 K; it is measured by coupling the half-cell with the standard hydrogen electrode.

**Relation to the equilibrium constant.** At equilibrium the cell does no further electrical work, so $E_{cell}=0$, and the Nernst equation

$$E=E^\circ-\frac{2.303RT}{nF}\log Q$$

becomes

$$0=E^\circ-\frac{0.0591}{n}\log K_c\ \Rightarrow\ E^\circ=\frac{0.0591}{n}\log K_c$$

(or, in natural logarithms, $\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ=-RT\ln K_c$). Hence $E^\circ$ is a direct measure of the equilibrium constant: a large positive $E^\circ$ means a large $K_c$.

**Numerical: Mg$^{2+}$/Mg at 0.01 M.** By the Nernst equation for the reduction $\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e^- -> Mg}$:

$$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.0591}{2}\log\frac{1}{[\ce{Mg^{2+}}]}=-2.36-\frac{0.0591}{2}\log\frac{1}{0.01}$$

$$=-2.36-\frac{0.0591}{2}\times2=-2.36-0.0591=-2.42\ \text{V}$$

**So the electrode potential is about −2.42 V** — slightly more negative than the standard value, as expected because the lowered Mg$^{2+}$ concentration makes the reduction still less favourable.

questions.question: Define the following terms: (i) Peptization (ii) Dialysis (iii) Hardy-Schultz law.
questions.answer:
**(i) Peptization** is the process of converting a freshly precipitated substance into a colloidal sol by shaking it with the dispersion medium in the presence of a small amount of an electrolyte (the *peptizing agent*). For example, a precipitate of Fe(OH)$_3$ is peptised by a little FeCl$_3$, which adsorbs on the particles and gives them like charges that keep them dispersed.

**(ii) Dialysis** is the removal of dissolved (true-solution) impurities from a colloidal sol by diffusion through a suitable semipermeable membrane such as parchment or cellophane. Small ions and molecules pass through the membrane into the surrounding water while the much larger colloidal particles cannot, so the sol is purified. (An electric field speeds this up — electrodialysis.)

**(iii) Hardy–Schulze law** states that the coagulating power of an ion is determined by its charge: the greater the valency of the flocculating ion added, the greater is its power to precipitate the sol. Thus for a negative sol the cations act, with coagulating power $\ce{Al^{3+}>Ba^{2+}>Na^{+}}$, and for a positive sol the anions, $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{4-}>PO4^{3-}>SO4^{2-}>Cl^{-}}$.

questions.question: Differentiate between mineral and ore.
questions.answer:
**Mineral** — a natural material in which a metal or its compound occurs in the earth's crust, together with the associated gangue. Every metal is extracted from a mineral, but **not every mineral is suitable** for extraction: many contain too little metal, or the compound is too difficult to reduce.

**Ore** — that mineral from which the metal can be extracted **conveniently and economically**. So every ore is a mineral, but not every mineral is an ore.

**Example:** the main minerals of copper are copper pyrites (CuFeS$_2$), copper glance (Cu$_2$S) and cuprite (Cu$_2$O) — also malachite, CuCO$_3$·Cu(OH)$_2$. Copper can be extracted profitably from the sulphide ones, so those are its ores; a copper-containing rock with only 0.1% metal would be a mineral but not an ore.

questions.question: Write down the I.U.P.A.C. names of the following ions: (i) [Mn(H$_2$O)$_6$]$^{2+}$Cl$_2$ (ii) K$_3$[Fe(CN)$_6$] (iii) [Cr(NH$_3$)$_6$]Cl$_3$
questions.answer:
**(i) [Mn(H$_2$O)$_6$]Cl$_2$** — the cation carries +2 with Mn in the +2 state and six aqua ligands: **hexaaquamanganese(II) chloride**.

**(ii) K$_3$[Fe(CN)$_6$]** — the anion carries −3, Fe is +3, six cyano ligands: **potassium hexacyanoferrate(III)**.

**(iii) [Cr(NH$_3$)$_6$]Cl$_3$** — the cation carries +3, Cr is +3, six ammine ligands: **hexaamminechromium(III) chloride**.

In each name the ligands are listed alphabetically before the metal name, the oxidation state appears as a Roman numeral in parentheses, and *-ate* is used for an anionic complex.

questions.question: How are carbohydrates classified?
questions.answer:
Carbohydrates are classified on the basis of their behaviour on hydrolysis into three groups:

1. **Monosaccharides** — the simplest sugars, which cannot be hydrolysed further; they are aldoses or ketoses with 3–7 carbons, e.g. **glucose** and **fructose** ($\ce{C6H12O6}$), ribose ($\ce{C5H10O5}$).
2. **Oligosaccharides** — give 2–10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis; they include the disaccharides such as **sucrose, maltose and lactose** ($\ce{C12H22O11}$).
3. **Polysaccharides** — give a large number of monosaccharide units on hydrolysis; **starch, cellulose and glycogen**, $\ce{(C6H10O5)_n}$, are the examples.

They may also be classified as reducing and non-reducing sugars according to whether the free aldehyde/ketone group is available — sucrose is non-reducing, glucose and maltose are reducing.

questions.question: Define the following terms with example: (i) Polyester (ii) Polyamide.
questions.answer:
**(i) Polyester** — a polymer formed by the condensation polymerisation of a dicarboxylic acid with a diol, with the elimination of water; the repeating linkage is the ester group, —COO—. The important example is **terylene (Dacron)**, from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid:

$$\ce{nHOCH2CH2OH + nHOOCC6H4COOH -> [-OCH2CH2OOC-C6H4-CO-]_n + 2nH2O}$$

Polyesters are strong, crease-resistant fibres used in clothing and as PET bottles.

**(ii) Polyamide** — a polymer in which the monomer units are joined by **amide linkages**, —CONH—, formed by condensing a diamine with a dicarboxylic acid. The important example is **Nylon-6,6**, from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid; Nylon-6 is the ring-opening polymer of caprolactam. Polyamides are strong fibres with high melting points because of hydrogen bonding between the chains.

questions.question: Derive integrated rate equation for a first order reaction. / The decomposition of NH$_3$ on platinum surface, $\ce{2NH3(g) -> N2(g) + 3H2(g)}$ is a zero order reaction with $k=2.5\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$. What are the rates of production of N$_2$ and H$_2$?
questions.answer:
**Integration of the first-order rate law.** For $\ce{R -> P}$ the rate law is

$$\text{rate}=-\frac{d[R]}{dt}=k[R]$$

Separating the variables and integrating from $t=0$ (concentration $[R]_0$) to $t$ (concentration $[R]$):

$$\int_{[R]_0}^{[R]}\frac{d[R]}{[R]}=-k\int_0^t dt$$

$$\ln[R]=-kt+\ln[R]_0$$

$$\ln\frac{[R]_0}{[R]}=kt\qquad\text{or}\qquad k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{[R]_0}{[R]}$$

Some consequences: a plot of $\log[R]$ against $t$ is a straight line of slope $-k/2.303$; the half-life $t_{1/2}=0.693/k$ is independent of the initial concentration; and the time for 99.9% completion is $10t_{1/2}$.

**Numerical (zero-order decomposition of NH$_3$).** For a zero-order reaction the rate is constant:

$$\text{rate}=k=2.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$$

From the stoichiometry $\ce{2NH3 -> N2 + 3H2}$, one mole of N$_2$ is produced per two moles of NH$_3$ decomposed, and three of H$_2$:

- Rate of production of **N$_2$** $=\frac12(2.5\times10^{-4})=1.25\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$
- Rate of production of **H$_2$** $=\frac32(2.5\times10^{-4})=3.75\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$

The rate of *decomposition* of ammonia is $2.5\times10^{-4}$, and the rate of the reaction (rate/$\nu$) is $1.25\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) $\ce{(NH4)2Cr2O7 ->[heat]}$ (ii) $\ce{C + HNO3(conc)}$ (iii) $\ce{(NH4)2SO4 + NaOH}$ (iv) $\ce{P4 + HNO3(conc)}$ (v) $\ce{P4 + NaOH + H2O}$
questions.answer:
**(i)** Ammonium dichromate decomposes violently on heating — the classic 'volcano' reaction, leaving green Cr$_2$O$_3$:

$$\ce{(NH4)2Cr2O7 ->[\Delta] Cr2O3 + N2 + 4H2O}$$

**(ii)** Carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide by hot concentrated nitric acid, which is reduced to NO$_2$:

$$\ce{C + 4HNO3(conc) -> CO2 + 4NO2 + 2H2O}$$

**(iii)** An ammonium salt with a strong base liberates ammonia:

$$\ce{(NH4)2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2NH3 ^ + 2H2O}$$

**(iv)** White phosphorus is oxidised to phosphoric acid:

$$\ce{P4 + 20HNO3(conc) -> 4H3PO4 + 20NO2 + 4H2O}$$

**(v)** Phosphorus with alkali disproportionates to phosphine and hypophosphite:

$$\ce{P4 + 3NaOH + 3H2O -> 3NaH2PO2 + PH3}$$

The last is the laboratory preparation of phosphine.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following transformations? (i) Butan-2-ol to Butanoic acid (ii) Bromobenzene to Benzoic acid (iii) Benzyl alcohol to Phenyl ethanoic acid (iv) Cyclohexene to Hexane-1,6-dioic acid (v) 1-Propanol to Propanal. / Write short notes on: (i) Aldol condensation (ii) Cannizzaro reaction.
questions.answer:
(i) **Butan-2-ol → butanoic acid:** oxidation to the ketone, then cleavage under strong oxidation:

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3 ->[K2Cr2O7/H2SO4] CH3CH2COCH3 ->[KMnO4/H^+][\Delta] CH3CH2COOH + CO2}$$

(ii) **Bromobenzene → benzoic acid:** via the Grignard reagent, which is then carbonated:

$$\ce{C6H5Br ->[Mg][dry ether] C6H5MgBr ->[CO2] C6H5COOMgBr ->[H3O^+] C6H5COOH}$$

(iii) **Benzyl alcohol → phenylethanoic acid:** convert to the chloride, then to the nitrile, and hydrolyse:

$$\ce{C6H5CH2OH ->[SOCl2] C6H5CH2Cl ->[KCN] C6H5CH2CN ->[H3O^+] C6H5CH2COOH}$$

(iv) **Cyclohexene → hexane-1,6-dioic acid (adipic acid):** oxidative cleavage of the double bond by hot alkaline permanganate opens the ring:

$$\ce{C6H10 ->[KMnO4/H2SO4][\Delta] HOOC(CH2)4COOH}$$

(v) **1-Propanol → propanal:** controlled oxidation with acidified dichromate, distilling off the aldehyde as it forms (or with PCC, which stops at the aldehyde):

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH ->[K2Cr2O7/H2SO4][\text{distil}] CH3CH2CHO}$$

**Short notes**

**(i) Aldol condensation.** In the presence of dilute alkali, a carbonyl compound with $\alpha$-hydrogens forms a carbanion that attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule; the product is a $\beta$-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone (an 'aldol'). On heating it loses water to give an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated carbonyl compound:

$$\ce{2CH3CHO ->[dil.NaOH] CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO ->[-H2O] CH3CH=CHCHO}$$

**(ii) Cannizzaro reaction.** An aldehyde with **no $\alpha$-hydrogen** (benzaldehyde, formaldehyde) undergoes disproportionation with concentrated alkali: one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate and another simultaneously reduced to the alcohol:

$$\ce{2C6H5CHO + NaOH -> C6H5CH2OH + C6H5COONa}$$

The mechanism involves hydride transfer from the intermediate alkoxide of the first molecule to the second.
